title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The rain had stopped, and now only mist hung in the air with drops still falling from the trees. Denisov, the esaul, and Petya rode in silence behind the peasant in the knitted cap, who stepped lightly on his turned-out feet, moving noiselessly in his bast shoes over roots and wet leaves as he led them to the forest's edge.
He climbed a rise, stopped, looked around, and moved toward a spot where the trees were thinner. Reaching a large oak that still held its leaves, he stopped and beckoned to them mysteriously.

Denisov and Petya rode up to him. From this spot they could see the French. Directly beyond the forest, on a downward slope, lay a field of spring rye. To the right, past a steep ravine, was a small village with a landowner's house whose roof had caved in. In the village, around the house, in the garden, by the well, by the pond, across all the rising ground, and along the road uphill from the bridge—no more than five hundred yards away—crowds of men could be seen through the shimmering mist. Their decidedly non-Russian shouts at horses straining uphill with carts, and their calls to one another, carried clearly.
'Bring the prisoner here,' said Denisov in a low voice, his eyes fixed on the French.

A Cossack dismounted, lifted the boy down, and brought him to Denisov. Pointing at the French troops, Denisov asked what these and those were. The boy, his cold hands thrust into his pockets and his eyebrows raised, looked at Denisov in fright but, despite an obvious desire to tell everything he knew, gave only confused answers, agreeing with whatever Denisov asked. Denisov turned away frowning and spoke to the esaul, sharing his own conclusions.
Petya kept turning his head rapidly—looking at the drummer boy, then at Denisov, then at the esaul, then at the French in the village and on the road—trying not to miss anything important.
'Whether Dolokhov comes or not, we have to take them—right?' said Denisov, his eyes sparkling with excitement.
'It's a very good position,' said the esaul.

'We'll send the infantry through the swamps,' Denisov continued. 'They'll creep up to the garden. You'll ride in from over there with the Cossacks'—he pointed to a spot in the forest beyond the village—'and I'll come from here with my hussars. And at the signal shot...'
'The ravine is impassable—there's a swamp there,' said the esaul. 'The horses would sink. We need to go further around to the left...'

While they were talking in undertones, a gunshot cracked from the low ground by the pond, a puff of white smoke appeared, then another, and the sound of hundreds of seemingly cheerful French voices shouting together rose from the slope. For a moment Denisov and the esaul pulled back. They were so close they thought the shooting was aimed at them. But the firing and shouting had nothing to do with them. Down below, a man in something red was running through the marsh. The French were obviously shooting and yelling at him.
'Why, that's our Tikhon,' said the esaul.
'So it is!'
'The rascal!' said Denisov.
'He'll get away!' said the esaul, squinting.

The man they called Tikhon ran to the stream and plunged in, sending up a splash of water. He disappeared for a moment, then scrambled out on all fours, black and dripping, and ran on. The French who had been chasing him stopped.
'Clever!' said the esaul.
'What a brute!' said Denisov with his earlier look of irritation. 'What's he been doing all this time?'
'Who is he?' asked Petya.
'He's our scout. I sent him to grab a "tongue."'
'Oh, yes,' said Petya, nodding at Denisov's first words as if he understood everything, though he really didn't understand any of it.

Tikhon Shcherbaty was one of the most indispensable men in their band. He was a peasant from Pokrovsk, near the Gzhat River. When Denisov had first come to Pokrovsk at the start of his operations and summoned the village elder to ask what he knew about the French, the elder—as all village elders did—claimed to have seen and heard nothing of them. But when Denisov explained that his purpose was to kill the French and asked whether any had strayed their way, the elder replied that some 'marauders' had indeed visited, but that Tikhon Shcherbaty was the only man who dealt with such matters. Denisov had Tikhon brought in and, after praising him for his activity, said a few words in the elder's presence about loyalty to the Tsar, love of country, and the hatred of the French that all sons of the fatherland should feel.

'We don't do the French any harm,' said Tikhon, clearly frightened by Denisov's words. 'We just messed around with the lads for fun, you know! We killed a couple dozen marauders, but we didn't do anything else...'

The next day, after Denisov had left Pokrovsk and completely forgotten about this peasant, word came that Tikhon had attached himself to their group and was asking to stay. Denisov gave orders to let him.

Tikhon, who at first did rough work—building campfires, fetching water, skinning dead horses—soon showed a great talent and enthusiasm for partisan warfare. At night he would go out raiding and always brought back French clothing and weapons, and when told to, brought in French captives as well. Denisov then relieved him from menial work, began taking him on expeditions, and had him enrolled among the Cossacks.

Tikhon didn't like riding and always went on foot, yet he never fell behind the cavalry. He carried a musket (mostly as a joke), a pike, and an axe, which he wielded the way a wolf uses its teeth—with equal ease picking fleas from its fur or crunching thick bones. Tikhon could split logs with full-arm swings just as accurately as he could whittle thin pegs or carve spoons. In Denisov's band, he held a unique position. When something particularly difficult or unpleasant had to be done—pushing a cart out of the mud with bare shoulders, pulling a horse out of a swamp by its tail, skinning it, sneaking into a French camp, or walking thirty miles in a day—everyone pointed laughingly at Tikhon.
'It won't hurt that devil—he's strong as a horse!' they said about him.

Once, a Frenchman Tikhon was trying to capture shot him in the fleshy part of his back. That wound—which Tikhon treated only with vodka, inside and out—became the subject of the liveliest jokes in the whole detachment, and Tikhon happily played along.

'Hey mate! Had enough? Gave you a good twist, did he?' the Cossacks would tease him. And Tikhon would deliberately writhe and make faces, pretending to be furious, swearing at the French with the funniest curses. The only lasting effect of the incident was that after being wounded, he rarely bothered bringing in prisoners.

He was the bravest and most useful man in the band. No one found more opportunities for attack, no one captured or killed more Frenchmen. And as a result, he became the butt of every joke among the Cossacks and hussars, a role he accepted willingly. Now Denisov had sent him overnight to Shamshevo to capture a 'tongue.' But whether because he hadn't been satisfied with taking just one Frenchman, or because he'd slept through the night, he had crept by day into the bushes right among the French and—as Denisov had witnessed from the hilltop—been spotted by them.
